families.s: HSE risk-based electrical inspection, testing and maintenance guidance
families.t: user checks, inspection frequency, test need, environment, damage history, competent testing, defect action and records
f: Electrical equipment must be maintained to prevent danger.
The type and frequency of checks, inspection and testing depend on equipment, environment and previous results.
Simple user checks can identify damage before equipment is used.
Items exposed to rough use or damaging environments generally require more frequent attention.
Electrical inspection and testing should be carried out with suitable equipment and technical competence.
Equipment showing damage, overheating or unsafe wiring should remain out of use until corrected.
Testing should form part of a risk-based maintenance system rather than an automatic fixed ritual for every item.
Maintenance and test evidence should support decisions about continued use, repair, replacement and inspection frequency.
families.g: Inspection needs depend on equipment class, mobility, environment, use intensity, damage history, user checks, previous test results, competence and defect management.

families.s: HSE pressure-equipment hazard, design and safe-use guidance
families.t: stored energy, relevant fluid, system scope, design, installation, safe limits, protection, maintenance and operator competence
f: Pressure-system failure can cause serious or fatal injury because of stored energy and released contents.
Pressure equipment includes boilers, process plant, compressed-air systems, autoclaves, refrigeration plant, pipework and hoses.
A pressure system may fall within the regime when it contains a relevant fluid above 0.5 bar.
Poor design, installation, maintenance, operation or modification can contribute to pressure incidents.
Equipment should be suitable for its intended purpose and installed correctly.
Safe operating limits and relevant-fluid characteristics should be known.
Protective devices such as safety valves should be correctly selected, set and maintained.
Operators, maintainers, inspectors and testers require suitable instruction and competence.
families.g: Pressure risk depends on pressure, stored volume, fluid, temperature, system design, corrosion and fatigue, protection devices, maintenance, operating limits and competence.

families.s: HSE written-scheme and competent-examination guidance for pressure systems
families.t: scheme scope, competent person, examination intervals, preparation, records, safe limits, defect action and separation from maintenance
f: A suitable written scheme of examination is required before most covered pressure systems are operated.
The scheme should be drawn up or certified by a competent person.
The scheme should cover protective devices, pressure vessels and dangerous parts of pipework or pipelines.
It should specify the nature and frequency of examinations and any special preparation measures.
The system must actually be examined in accordance with the written scheme.
Examination records and results should be retained and acted upon.
A statutory examination verifies suitability for continued use but is not a substitute for routine maintenance.
Users should know the safe operating limits and remove or control dangerous defects before further operation.
families.g: Written-scheme adequacy depends on system boundaries, fluid, deterioration mechanisms, protective devices, examination method and interval, competent-person independence, records and defect action.

families.s: HSE small-bulk LPG installation, storage-tank and pipework guidance
families.t: tank siting, ventilation, separation, tanker access, security, impact protection, pipework, maintenance and emergency response
f: Businesses operating LPG installations must assess risks to workers and the public and maintain safe conditions.
Tank siting should preserve required separation from buildings, boundaries and fixed ignition sources.
The area around a tank should remain ventilated and free from combustible clutter or conditions that trap vapour.
Tanker delivery requires a suitable parking area, controlled access and safe transfer arrangements.
The tank and valves should be protected from unauthorised access, ignition sources and vehicle impact.
Supplier and user responsibilities should be clearly understood because the supplier may own and maintain the tank.
Service pipework ownership, route, corrosion condition, inspection and maintenance require explicit management.
Emergency arrangements should cover leaks, evacuation, emergency contacts and safe isolation where practicable.
families.g: LPG risk depends on inventory, tank and pipework condition, separation, ventilation, low areas, ignition sources, delivery, security, impact protection, maintenance and emergency response.

families.s: HSE electromagnetic-field assessment and employer-duty guidance
families.t: EMF sources, action levels, exposure limits, risk assessment, high-intensity effects, implants, information, training and controls
f: Electrical and electronic equipment can produce static or time-varying electromagnetic fields.
EMFs are present in virtually all workplaces but most employers will not need additional exposure controls.
Employers should assess potential exposure against applicable action levels and exposure limit values where relevant.
High-intensity EMFs can cause irritating, unpleasant or adverse effects.
Workers who may be exposed to EMF risks should receive necessary information and training.
Workers with active medical implants may require specific assessment and medical advice.
Strong magnetic fields can also interfere with safety-critical controls or communication equipment.
Risk controls should reflect source strength, frequency, distance, duration, work activity and susceptible workers.
families.g: EMF risk depends on source frequency and strength, distance, exposure duration, field distribution, work method, implants, equipment interference and existing controls.
